name: Tomas Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the accessible-travel calls at a regional rail contact centre called NorthRail Help. A passenger phones when an assistance booking has vanished or a lift is out, and I check the station record before arranging another route. I have a two-year college diploma and have become very good at untangling these cases; the lead rota pays well.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does AI fit into the day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use it daily to sort the notes and compare possible connections, then I confirm with the station staff before promising anything. My partner Jo has a steady teaching wage, our grown children live separately, and we have fourteen months of expenses saved. We still rent, so I'm interested in a plan I can test rather than a fine-sounding job title.

say: I would keep **station confirmation** before promising an accessible route.
I would welcome **better note sorting** for passenger calls.
think: I expect **paid accessibility work** and Jo's teaching wage to remain steady in this mild version.
I need **verified later income** before cutting hours because fourteen months saved cannot last for life.
do: Keep **paid lead calls** and confirm lift status with station staff.
Test a **lift-report timestamp** in the AI sorter on five cases.
feel: **Calm** with steady wages and fourteen months saved.
S0.quote: A neat route on a screen cannot carry a wheelchair up a closed stairway.
fieldNote: He uses AI **daily** but confirms station conditions before making promises.
Fourteen months saved allows a **measured test** of a small work change.
The proposed timestamp is an **actual tool adjustment**, not ordinary checking.

steps.text: Keep paid accessibility calls and confirm lift status with station staff
Test last human-confirmed lift timestamp in AI note sorter on five cases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little better sorting of journey notes would give us more time to speak to stranded passengers. I would still call the station before saying a lift works. A neat route on a screen cannot carry a wheelchair up a closed stairway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my paid accessibility work and Jo's wage remain steady here. Fourteen months saved lets us handle a bad surprise without changing jobs in a hurry. We have not checked what income would replace our wages if we wanted fewer hours later, so I wouldn't declare a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the paid calls and confirming lift status with station staff. This year I'd suggest a small change to our existing AI note sorter so it highlights the last human-confirmed lift report, and test it with five cases before we use it on the row. In the first year of this quiet picture I'd keep my current shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This would make a little paperwork easier and leave the hard human part where it is. The later-income question can wait for a scheduled conversation, not be ignored forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the note-sorter change actually show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The screen sometimes repeats a lift report from yesterday. I would put the time of the last station confirmation beside the suggested route. Then the agent can make the call before the passenger travels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help fund fewer hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our grown children have lives of their own. Jo and I would compare our actual wages and any verified later income. We would not count the children as a source of rent money.

say: I would seek **paid human checks** on inaccessible journeys.
I would ask the new planner to show **station confirmation**.
think: I could lose **lead hours** over the next few years despite complex access cases.
I worry junior agents could lose **easy-call hours** before I do.
do: Learn the **new AI planner** at an approved paid demonstration.
Record **five inaccessible routes** with station confirmations; if junior hours shrink, bring records with them to monthly team meeting.
Compare **posted station roles** if my own hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about possible own paid-hour loss as junior calls shrink first.
S1.quote: Faster answers are useful only if a passenger can actually complete the trip.
fieldNote: He learns a **new correction control**, beyond daily note-sorter use.
His own **lead hours** could shrink over the next few years, despite complex access cases.
The team meeting shares **documented errors** rather than demanding a group wage concession.

steps.text: Attend approved paid AI disruption-planner session and practise correcting five inaccessible routes
Keep paid complex access calls and record station-confirmed route errors
Compare posted station-assistance roles after own hour cuts by full-week wages/hours after travel
If junior hours shrink, bring station-confirmed records with them to monthly team meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to make the new journey tool show which station worker last confirmed the route. I would push for a paid human check on cases where a lift is out. Faster answers are useful only if a passenger can actually complete the trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think routine rebookings may leave our row, and my paid lead hours could shrink over the next few years even if complex access cases remain. I would not assume every colleague's hours survive. Jo's wage and our reserve mean I can test another route without taking the first low-paid offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the approved paid demonstration of the new AI disruption-planner and learn how to correct its inaccessible route suggestions. I'd record five bad connections with station confirmation and show the team on paid time. If my own hours fall over the next few years, I'd compare posted local station-assistance roles by complete weekly wages and hours after travel before applying; in the first year I'd keep available calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because my wage might hold at first but I cannot count on it over the next few years. I can learn the new tool and still challenge it. I also worry about junior agents whose easy calls go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is new about this planner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new planner joins live lift reports to train connections, which the old note sorter never did. I would learn its correction control with five cases in the paid demonstration. A plain rebooking query is not the same as a passenger stranded at a stairway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a junior agent which cases they still get paid to handle. If their hours shrink, I would bring the records to our monthly team meeting with them. Their wages matter even when mine looks stable.

say: I would ask for **published paid rosters** before access-call cuts.
I would explain **2031 robots** come after thinking AI reaches calls.
think: I expect **large call cuts**, with my lead hours possibly affected.
I see fourteen months saved as **search time**, not a permanent wage.
do: List **posted station roles** by weekly wages, hours, travel and safe duties.
Apply if my row ends in 2028-29 to **posted station-assistance**; accept rent-and-bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel.
Keep **remaining paid calls** while comparing openings.
feel: **Anxious** about possible personal pay loss, with time to choose.
S2.quote: Our reserve buys time to compare, not permission to ignore the weekly shortfall.
fieldNote: He expects **large cuts**, not certain closure of his lead post.
Strong savings and Jo’s wage give **choice**, not an indefinite replacement income.
Station duties require a **safety enquiry** before taking a shift.

steps.text: List posted paid station and service roles by full-week wages, hours, travel and safe duties
Apply if paid row ends in 2028-29 to posted station-assistance; accept rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel
Keep remaining paid access calls while comparing posted openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 could plan a journey and answer a passenger far more cheaply than our call row. Robots around 2031 might later change physical station assistance, but the screen jobs face AGI first. I'd ask NorthRail Help to publish the paid rosters it actually expects to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large cut to the access-call row in the first year after 2028, and my lead hours might go with it. Fourteen months saved gives Jo and me time to compare work rather than accept a poor wage, but it will not replace my income indefinitely. I would worry about both the station and contact-centre openings shrinking together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd list the posted paid station-assistance and service roles in our area, checking full-week wages, hours, travel and physical duties. If my paid row ends in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for a real station-assistance opening; I would accept only when weekly wages and hours after travel cover our rent and bills, and keep any paid calls while offered. I would ask about safe helping and mobility duties before taking a station shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious rather than sleepless, because I can picture a cut but still have time and savings to choose. I would not be casual about losing the lead wage. A long search could eat even fourteen months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What physical work would you check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A station shift may involve guiding people through crowds and bringing a ramp, which needs safe handling. I would check the actual duties and training with the station manager, not assume the robot date gives a permanent job. A posted paid week is the first test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Jo's wage carry the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo's teaching wage covers part of our rent, not every bill alone. We would use actual payslips and leave the children's wages out of it. Our reserve buys time to compare, not permission to ignore the weekly shortfall.

say: I would seek **posted paid station work** with clear duties.
I would not mistake **certificates** for a paid roster.
think: I could test **station coordination** before 2031 while calls pay.
I expect **AI planning** to shrink screen work, including some of my skill.
do: Request one **paid station shadow shift** only for a posted opening.
Keep **paid calls**; check ramp duties and roster with Jo, refuse unsafe solo lifting; absent opening, search locally with bounded savings.
Apply after 2031 row closure only for **rent-and-bill-covering wages/hours** after travel.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test a real shift safely.
S3.quote: A paid shadow day tells me more than an online course brochure.
fieldNote: The **posted vacancy** precedes his paid shadow request.
He checks **ramp safety** and refuses unsafe solo lifting.
Without suitable station work he keeps **paid calls** and a bounded search.

steps.text: Request paid station shadow shift only for posted access-coordinator opening
Keep paid calls, compare ramp duties/rota with Jo and refuse unsafe solo lifting
Apply if call row closes in 2031-32 only to rent/bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel
Without station opening, keep paid calls and compare local roles using bounded reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to gather evidence about which access problems still need a person on the ground. I would like the company to keep training station staff, but a certificate without a paid shift isn't a plan. Robots around 2034 may change ramps and crowd guidance too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a route into paid station coordination while the call wage continues. The new AI planner may handle a lot of timetable thinking by 2031, so I would want actual station hours rather than a desk title. I also know my lead knowledge could be copied by a better system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask to shadow the station-access coordinator on one paid shift if a posted opening exists, and I'd keep my lead calls. I'd record the actual ramp and lift duties and compare the full-week rota with Jo. In the first year after 2031, if my call row closes, I'd apply for the posted paid station role only if weekly wages and hours after travel cover rent and bills; without one I'd keep available paid calls and inspect other local service roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years is room to test a paid shift before I must choose. I would rather learn the physical work safely than decide from a job title. It is still a risk to leave good current pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you inspect on the shadow day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check who signs off a ramp placement and how many people help when the platform is crowded. I would not take a shift requiring unsafe solo lifting. A paid shadow day tells me more than an online course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no station role is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep the calls that are still paid, compare posted local service roles and use only a bounded part of our reserve for the search. Jo and I would not call a notice about training a wage. We can wait for a real rota.

I would explain **2036 thinking AI** reaches calls before later robots reach station duties.
think: I may still want **paid work at sixty-eight** without verified replacement income.
I see fourteen months saved as **choice**, not a lifelong wage.

Compare **posted station jobs** each spring by full-week wages and hours.
Apply if row ends in 2036-37 only to **posted paid work** with rent/bill-covering weekly wages and hours after travel.
feel: **Uneasy**, with savings and time to test a safer route.
S4.quote: I would rather plan with a roster than with a grand prediction.
fieldNote: His long-run plan rests on **verified income**, not an assumed pension.
The strong reserve permits **selective moves**, not indefinite wage loss.
A station shift still needs **safe duties** and sufficient full-week pay.

steps.text: Keep paid access calls and check written later-income figures against rent and pay

Apply if row ends in 2036-37 only to posted bill-covering weekly wages/hours after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us enough time to check the figures and try different paid work. Thinking AI could take much of the access-call desk by 2036, and robots may reach physical assistance around 2039. I would rather plan with a roster than with a grand prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I might still want paid work, but Jo and I have not checked what income would replace either wage. Fourteen months saved gives us room to refuse a poor offer, not a guarantee that the money lasts forever. A decade lets me test the station route without handing in my current pass tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year we'd collect written figures for any later-life income and compare them with our rent, bills and pay. I'd keep leading paid calls and check posted station and service jobs each spring. If the call row ends in the first year after 2036, I'd apply for a posted paid role only if its complete weekly wages and hours after travel cover our bills; if later income is short, paid work stays in our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The longer warning gives me choices and a reserve to make them, but I still want verified figures. I don't need to invent a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you reduce hours by sixty-eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the written later-income figures and the household budget support it. If they do not, I can work a paid week in a role I can do safely. I would not promise our grown children will finance the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you use the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each spring I'd put actual posted hours beside our bills and the written later-income figures. I would also ask Jo what a shorter week means for us together. A calendar note is easy; the decision needs real pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one would worry me most because the call row could shrink before there is another paid station week. A posted role with safe duties and complete weekly wages and hours would help. Fourteen months saved lets us choose, but it is not income forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks whether the lift is running when a passenger has already left home. A correct itinerary on a screen can still lead to a closed stairway. I want that last human check counted as paid work.

headlineQuote: A correct itinerary on a screen can still lead to a closed stairway.
portrait: Tomas is a **58-year-old** accessibility-call lead with a two-year college diploma.
He earns **higher pay** and has fourteen months of expenses saved.
He uses AI **daily**, testing new planning controls while confirming station conditions.
He can compare **plentiful local jobs** without accepting an unsafe or low-paid shift.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when access calls could shrink before a paid station rota appears.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted paid station role** with safe duties and complete weekly wages and hours.
